claim: TPR is a protein of the nuclear pore complex basket required for heterochromatin re-organisation during senescence.
source: Here, we show that TPR, a protein of the nuclear pore complex basket required for heterochromatin re-organisation during senescence, is also required for the very early activation of NF-κB signalling during the stress-response phase of oncogene-induced senescence.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by references to prior work (Boumendil et al., 2019) and experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: TPR is required for the very early activation of NF-κB signalling during the stress-response phase of oncogene-induced senescence.
source: Here, we show that TPR, a protein of the nuclear pore complex basket required for heterochromatin re-organisation during senescence, is also required for the very early activation of NF-κB signalling during the stress-response phase of oncogene-induced senescence.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing decreased NF-κB activation at early timepoints (d3 and d5) upon TPR knockdown.

claim: TPR-dependent early NF-κB activation occurs prior to activation of the SASP.
source: This is prior to activation of the SASP and occurs without affecting NF-κB nuclear import.
evidence: This is supported by data showing NF-κB activation at d3 and d5, which are before SASP induction.

claim: TPR-dependent early NF-κB activation occurs without affecting NF-κB nuclear import.
source: This is prior to activation of the SASP and occurs without affecting NF-κB nuclear import.
evidence: This is supported by conditioned media experiments showing that TPR knockdown does not prevent NF-κB nuclear translocation when cells are exposed to SASP factors.

claim: TPR is required for the activation of innate immune signalling at early stages of senescence.
source: We show that TPR is required for the activation of innate immune signalling at these early stages of senescence and we link this to the formation of heterochromatin-enriched cytoplasmic chromatin fragments thought to bleb off from the nuclear periphery.
evidence: This is supported by data showing decreased STING expression, TBK1 phosphorylation, and cGAMP production upon TPR knockdown.

claim: TPR is required for the formation of heterochromatin-enriched cytoplasmic chromatin fragments.
source: We show that TPR is required for the activation of innate immune signalling at these early stages of senescence and we link this to the formation of heterochromatin-enriched cytoplasmic chromatin fragments thought to bleb off from the nuclear periphery.
evidence: This is supported by data showing decreased CCF frequency upon TPR knockdown at d5 of OIS.

claim: HMGA1 is required for cytoplasmic chromatin fragment formation.
source: We show that HMGA1 is also required for cytoplasmic chromatin fragment formation.
evidence: This is supported by data showing decreased CCF frequency upon HMGA1 knockdown at d5 of OIS.

claim: Re-organisation of heterochromatin is involved in altered structural integrity of the nuclear periphery during senescence.
source: Together these data suggest that re-organisation of heterochromatin is involved in altered structural integrity of the nuclear periphery during senescence, and that this can lead to activation of cytoplasmic nucleic acid sensing, NF-κB signalling, and activation of the SASP.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both TPR and HMGA1, which are required for SAHF formation, are also required for CCF formation.

claim: Altered structural integrity of the nuclear periphery during senescence can lead to activation of cytoplasmic nucleic acid sensing, NF-κB signalling, and activation of the SASP.
source: Together these data suggest that re-organisation of heterochromatin is involved in altered structural integrity of the nuclear periphery during senescence, and that this can lead to activation of cytoplasmic nucleic acid sensing, NF-κB signalling, and activation of the SASP.
evidence: This is inferred from the data linking CCF formation to innate immune signalling and NF-κB activation.

claim: During oncogene-induced senescence, pre-existing heterochromatin moves away from the nuclear periphery.
source: During oncogene-induced senescence (OIS) chromatin organisation is dramatically disrupted. Pre-existing heterochromatin moves away from the nuclear periphery (Chandra et al., 2012), forming internal senescence-associated heterochromatic foci (SAHF) (Narita et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Pre-existing heterochromatin forms internal senescence-associated heterochromatic foci (SAHF) during oncogene-induced senescence.
source: During oncogene-induced senescence (OIS) chromatin organisation is dramatically disrupted. Pre-existing heterochromatin moves away from the nuclear periphery (Chandra et al., 2012), forming internal senescence-associated heterochromatic foci (SAHF) (Narita et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Senescent cells activate a gene expression programme that leads to the secretion of inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and growth factors known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP).
source: Senescent cells also activate a gene expression programme that leads to the secretion of a cocktail of inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and growth factors – known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) (Coppé et al., 2010; Acosta et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The SASP can contribute to tumour suppression by enhancing immune cell recruitment.
source: The SASP can contribute to tumour suppression by enhancing immune cell recruitment (Kale et al., 2020; Xue et al., 2007), but it can also promote tumour growth (Kuilman et al., 2008) and immunosuppression (Ruhland et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The SASP can promote tumour growth.
source: The SASP can contribute to tumour suppression by enhancing immune cell recruitment (Kale et al., 2020; Xue et al., 2007), but it can also promote tumour growth (Kuilman et al., 2008) and immunosuppression (Ruhland et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The SASP can promote immunosuppression.
source: The SASP can contribute to tumour suppression by enhancing immune cell recruitment (Kale et al., 2020; Xue et al., 2007), but it can also promote tumour growth (Kuilman et al., 2008) and immunosuppression (Ruhland et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Activation of SASP-related genes is primarily driven by the transcription factors NF-κB (subunit p65) and C/EBPβ.
source: Activation of SASP-related genes is primarily driven by the transcription factors (TFs) NF-κB (subunit p65) and C/EBPβ (Chien et al., 2011; Kuilman et al., 2008) and is accompanied by substantial changes in the landscape of active enhancers (Martínez-Zamudio et al., 2020; Tasdemir et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Activation of SASP-related genes is accompanied by substantial changes in the landscape of active enhancers.
source: Activation of SASP-related genes is primarily driven by the transcription factors (TFs) NF-κB (subunit p65) and C/EBPβ (Chien et al., 2011; Kuilman et al., 2008) and is accompanied by substantial changes in the landscape of active enhancers (Martínez-Zamudio et al., 2020; Tasdemir et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Heterochromatin blebs off from the nuclear membrane during OIS, forming cytoplasmic chromatin fragments (CCFs).
source: As well as relocating to the nuclear interior to form SAHF, heterochromatin blebs off from the nuclear membrane during OIS, forming cytoplasmic chromatin fragments (CCFs) (Ivanov et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: CCFs are enriched for the heterochromatin-associated histone modifications H3K9me3 and H3K27me3.
source: CCFs are enriched for the heterochromatin-associated histone modifications H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 (Dou et al., 2017; Ivanov et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and confirmed by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5B.

claim: CCFs are positive for γ-H2AX, suggesting that DNA damage plays a role in CCF formation.
source: CCFs are also positive for γ-H2AX, suggesting that DNA damage plays a role in CCF formation (Ivanov et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and confirmed by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5C.

claim: In the cytoplasm, CCFs are sensed by the cGAS-STING pathway, which leads to activation of the SASP via NF-κB signalling.
source: In the cytoplasm, CCFs are sensed by the cGAS-STING pathway, which leads to activation of the SASP via NF-κB signalling (Dou et al., 2017; Glück et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: TPR excludes heterochromatin from the vicinity of nuclear pores.
source: We have previously shown that the nuclear pore basket protein TPR, that excludes heterochromatin from the vicinity of nuclear pores (Krull et al., 2010), is necessary for both the formation and maintenance of SAHF, as well as for activation of the SASP, during OIS (Boumendil et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: TPR is necessary for both the formation and maintenance of SAHF during OIS.
source: We have previously shown that the nuclear pore basket protein TPR, that excludes heterochromatin from the vicinity of nuclear pores (Krull et al., 2010), is necessary for both the formation and maintenance of SAHF, as well as for activation of the SASP, during OIS (Boumendil et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: TPR is necessary for activation of the SASP during OIS.
source: We have previously shown that the nuclear pore basket protein TPR, that excludes heterochromatin from the vicinity of nuclear pores (Krull et al., 2010), is necessary for both the formation and maintenance of SAHF, as well as for activation of the SASP, during OIS (Boumendil et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: HMGA1 is a component of SAHFs.
source: The AT-hook chromatin protein HMGA1 has similarly been shown to be a component of SAHFs and to be required for SAHF formation (Narita et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: HMGA1 is required for SAHF formation.
source: The AT-hook chromatin protein HMGA1 has similarly been shown to be a component of SAHFs and to be required for SAHF formation (Narita et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and confirmed by data in Figure 5F-G.

claim: TPR is a 267 kDa protein.
source: TPR is a 267 kDa protein (Figure 1A) added to the nuclear pore late in telophase after other nuclear pore components and is anchored to the nuclear pore basket through its interaction with NUP153 (Hase and Cordes, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A, supported by citation.

claim: TPR is added to the nuclear pore late in telophase after other nuclear pore components.
source: TPR is a 267 kDa protein (Figure 1A) added to the nuclear pore late in telophase after other nuclear pore components and is anchored to the nuclear pore basket through its interaction with NUP153 (Hase and Cordes, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: TPR is anchored to the nuclear pore basket through its interaction with NUP153.
source: TPR is a 267 kDa protein (Figure 1A) added to the nuclear pore late in telophase after other nuclear pore components and is anchored to the nuclear pore basket through its interaction with NUP153 (Hase and Cordes, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Knockdown or degradation of TPR does not affect NUP153 recruitment to the nuclear pore.
source: Knockdown or degradation of TPR has been shown not to affect NUP153 recruitment to the nuclear pore (Hase and Cordes, 2003; Aksenova et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The chromatin regulatory landscape of IMR90 cells changes during OIS.
source: The chromatin regulatory landscape of IMR90 cells changes during OIS (Tasdemir et al., 2016) and there is evidence that some nucleoporins interact with enhancers and regulate the transcriptional activity of associated genes (Ibarra et al., 2016; Pascual-Garcia et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Some nucleoporins interact with enhancers and regulate the transcriptional activity of associated genes.
source: The chromatin regulatory landscape of IMR90 cells changes during OIS (Tasdemir et al., 2016) and there is evidence that some nucleoporins interact with enhancers and regulate the transcriptional activity of associated genes (Ibarra et al., 2016; Pascual-Garcia et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Of the 6826 peaks with a significant increase in accessibility in senescent compared to non-senescent control cells, 1187 are also TPR-dependent.
source: Of the 6826 peaks with a significant increase in accessibility in senescent (RAS siCTRL) compared to non-senescent control (STOP siCTRL) cells (senescent-dependent (SEN+)), 1187 are also TPR-dependent (SEN+TPR+) (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Many TPR-dependent senescence-specific accessible chromatin regions are close to key SASP genes, such as IL1B and IL8.
source: Many of these are close to key SASP genes, such as IL1B and IL8 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq track views shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Both SEN+TPR+ and SEN+TPR- peak categories showed an increase in H3K27 acetylation in senescent IMR90 RASG12V cells when compared with the non-senescent control.
source: Both SEN+TPR+ and SEN+TPR- peak categories showed an increase in H3K27 acetylation (H3K27ac), as assayed from ChIP-seq data (Parry et al., 2018), in senescent IMR90 ER:HRASG12V cells when compared with the non-senescent control (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of published ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The regions which become accessible upon senescence may function as senescence-specific enhancers, regardless of their dependence on TPR.
source: This suggests that the regions which become accessible upon senescence may function as senescence-specific enhancers, regardless of their dependence on TPR.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both TPR-dependent and TPR-independent senescence-specific peaks show increased H3K27ac.

claim: TPR-dependent peaks are significantly near to known SASP factor genes.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis carried out using the Genomic Regions Enrichment of Annotations Tool (GREAT) (McLean et al., 2010) showed that TPR-dependent peaks are significantly near to known SASP factor genes, and to genes enriched in Biological Process and Molecular Function categories such as 'positive regulation of inflammatory response', and genes involved in cytokine activity and cytokine receptor binding (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: TPR-dependent peaks are near to genes enriched in Biological Process and Molecular Function categories such as 'positive regulation of inflammatory response', and genes involved in cytokine activity and cytokine receptor binding.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis carried out using the Genomic Regions Enrichment of Annotations Tool (GREAT) (McLean et al., 2010) showed that TPR-dependent peaks are significantly near to known SASP factor genes, and to genes enriched in Biological Process and Molecular Function categories such as 'positive regulation of inflammatory response', and genes involved in cytokine activity and cytokine receptor binding (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: TPR-independent senescent-dependent peaks showed proximity to chemokine receptor genes (XCR1, CCR1).
source: TPR-independent senescent-dependent peaks showed proximity to chemokine receptor genes (XCR1, CCR1) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) whose expression allows cells to sense and respond to chemokines such as those secreted in the SASP (Coppé et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: TPR-independent peaks did not show proximity to any SASP factor genes.
source: However, the TPR-independent peaks did not show proximity to any SASP factor genes, suggesting that senescence-activated regulatory elements close to SASP genes (Tasdemir et al., 2016) may all be TPR-dependent.
evidence: This is inferred from the GO analysis results.

claim: Senescence-activated regulatory elements close to SASP genes may all be TPR-dependent.
source: However, the TPR-independent peaks did not show proximity to any SASP factor genes, suggesting that senescence-activated regulatory elements close to SASP genes (Tasdemir et al., 2016) may all be TPR-dependent.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TPR-independent peaks do not show proximity to SASP factor genes.

claim: d8 SEN+TPR+, but not TPR-independent (SEN+TPR-), ATAC-seq peaks are enriched for binding motifs of TFs, such as NF-κB and C/EBPβ, known to regulate the SASP.
source: HOMER motif analysis (Heinz et al., 2010) revealed that d8 SEN+TPR+, but not TPR-independent (SEN+TPR-), ATAC-seq peaks are enriched for binding motifs of TFs, such as NF-κB and C/EBPβ, known to regulate the SASP (Acosta et al., 2008; Kuilman et al., 2008; Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by HOMER motif analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: TPR is involved in regulation of the NF-κB-dependent pro-inflammatory SASP during OIS.
source: This indicates that TPR is involved in regulation of the NF-κB-dependent pro-inflammatory SASP during OIS.
evidence: This is inferred from the enrichment of NF-κB binding motifs in TPR-dependent peaks.

claim: Both categories of senescent-dependent peaks are enriched in binding motifs for components of the AP-1 complex.
source: Both categories of senescent-dependent peaks are enriched in binding motifs for components of the AP-1 complex (Figure 1E), a pioneer TF premarking prospective senescence enhancers (Martínez-Zamudio et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by HOMER motif analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: AP-1 is a pioneer TF premarking prospective senescence enhancers.
source: Both categories of senescent-dependent peaks are enriched in binding motifs for components of the AP-1 complex (Figure 1E), a pioneer TF premarking prospective senescence enhancers (Martínez-Zamudio et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The initial shaping of the senescence regulatory landscape by AP-1 is unaffected by TPR knockdown.
source: This suggests that the initial shaping of the senescence regulatory landscape by AP-1 is unaffected by TPR knockdown.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both TPR-dependent and TPR-independent peaks are enriched for AP-1 binding motifs.

claim: Inactive NF-κB dimers are held in the cytoplasm through their association with IκB proteins.
source: Inactive NF-κB dimers are held in the cytoplasm through their association with IκB proteins. Inducing stimuli trigger activation of the IκB kinase complex (IKK), which leads to phosphorylation and degradation of IκB, allowing the translocation of NF-κB to the nucleus, where it promotes the transcription of target genes (Hayden and Ghosh, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about NF-κB signaling, supported by citation.

claim: Inducing stimuli trigger activation of the IκB kinase complex (IKK), which leads to phosphorylation and degradation of IκB, allowing the translocation of NF-κB to the nucleus.
source: Inactive NF-κB dimers are held in the cytoplasm through their association with IκB proteins. Inducing stimuli trigger activation of the IκB kinase complex (IKK), which leads to phosphorylation and degradation of IκB, allowing the translocation of NF-κB to the nucleus, where it promotes the transcription of target genes (Hayden and Ghosh, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about NF-κB signaling, supported by citation.

claim: NF-κB in the nucleus promotes the transcription of target genes.
source: Inactive NF-κB dimers are held in the cytoplasm through their association with IκB proteins. Inducing stimuli trigger activation of the IκB kinase complex (IKK), which leads to phosphorylation and degradation of IκB, allowing the translocation of NF-κB to the nucleus, where it promotes the transcription of target genes (Hayden and Ghosh, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about NF-κB signaling, supported by citation.

claim: NF-κB remains cytoplasmic in control (STOP) cells.
source: As expected, NF-κB remained cytoplasmic in control (STOP) cells, but translocation to the nucleus could be detected in senescent RAS cells, with SAHF readily apparent from DAPI staining in the nucleus of these cells.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: NF-κB translocates to the nucleus in senescent RAS cells.
source: As expected, NF-κB remained cytoplasmic in control (STOP) cells, but translocation to the nucleus could be detected in senescent RAS cells, with SAHF readily apparent from DAPI staining in the nucleus of these cells.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: SAHF are readily apparent from DAPI staining in the nucleus of senescent RAS cells.
source: As expected, NF-κB remained cytoplasmic in control (STOP) cells, but translocation to the nucleus could be detected in senescent RAS cells, with SAHF readily apparent from DAPI staining in the nucleus of these cells.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Knockdown of TPR in RAS cells blocks SAHF formation.
source: As we previously reported, knockdown of TPR (siTPR) in RAS cells blocks SAHF formation, but it also results in reduced nuclear localisation (decreased nucleocytoplasmic ratio) of NF-κB, consistent with decreased NF-κB activation (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A and prior work.

claim: Knockdown of TPR in RAS cells results in reduced nuclear localisation (decreased nucleocytoplasmic ratio) of NF-κB.
source: As we previously reported, knockdown of TPR (siTPR) in RAS cells blocks SAHF formation, but it also results in reduced nuclear localisation (decreased nucleocytoplasmic ratio) of NF-κB, consistent with decreased NF-κB activation (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Active NF-κB is phosphorylated at serine 536.
source: Active NF-κB is phosphorylated at serine 536 (Sakurai et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge about NF-κB, supported by citation.

claim: Phosphorylation of NF-κB is increased in RAS cells compared with the STOP control cells.
source: Immunoblotting showed that, as expected, phosphorylation of NF-κB is increased in RAS cells compared with the STOP control cells.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In RAS cells, phosphorylation of NF-κB, but not total levels of NF-κB, decreased upon TPR knockdown.
source: In RAS cells phosphorylation of NF-κB, but not total levels of NF-κB, decreased upon TPR knockdown (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Phosphorylation of the NF-κB kinase IKK was reduced in RAS cells upon TPR knockdown.
source: Phosphorylation of the NF-κB kinase IKK, and total levels of IKKα, were also reduced in RAS cells upon TPR knockdown (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), further suggesting a reduction in NF-κB signalling pathway activation in senescent cells in the absence of TPR.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Total levels of IKKα were reduced in RAS cells upon TPR knockdown.
source: Phosphorylation of the NF-κB kinase IKK, and total levels of IKKα, were also reduced in RAS cells upon TPR knockdown (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), further suggesting a reduction in NF-κB signalling pathway activation in senescent cells in the absence of TPR.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: CM from senescent RAS cells is enriched in SASP factors which leads to NF-κB activation.
source: CM from senescent RAS cells is enriched in SASP factors which leads to NF-κB activation (Boumendil et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Nuclear translocation of NF-κB occurs in RAS cells (with control siRNA) in the presence of CM from either STOP or RAS cells.
source: Immunofluorescence showed that nuclear translocation of NF-κB occurs in RAS cells (with control siRNA) in the presence of CM from either STOP or RAS cells, because of their intrinsic activation of the SASP.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: In STOP cells, nuclear translocation of NF-κB was only induced by CM from RAS cells.
source: In STOP cells, nuclear translocation of NF-κB was only induced by CM from RAS cells.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Nuclear translocation of NF-κB induced by CM from RAS cells was not affected by TPR knockdown.
source: This was not affected by TPR knockdown, and this was also the case for RAS cells after TPR knockdown (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2E and quantification in Figure 2F.

claim: TPR knockdown does not affect the nuclear import of NF-κB.
source: Quantification of the NF-κB nucleocytoplasmic ratio confirms that TPR knockdown does not affect the nuclear import of NF-κB (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The SASP reinforces itself via a positive feedback loop.
source: The SASP reinforces itself via a positive feedback loop – once secreted, SASP factors bind to receptors on the cell membrane, leading to NF-κB activation and increased SASP (Figure 3A; Acosta et al., 2008; Freund et al., 2010; Orjalo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: Once secreted, SASP factors bind to receptors on the cell membrane, leading to NF-κB activation and increased SASP.
source: The SASP reinforces itself via a positive feedback loop – once secreted, SASP factors bind to receptors on the cell membrane, leading to NF-κB activation and increased SASP (Figure 3A; Acosta et al., 2008; Freund et al., 2010; Orjalo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Day 3 (d3) is before SASP induction and occurs when the cells are coming out of the initial highly proliferative state.
source: To determine whether this was the case, we assessed NF-κB nuclear localisation at two earlier timepoints: day 3 (d3), which is before SASP induction and occurs when the cells are coming out of the initial highly proliferative state (Young et al., 2009), and day 5 (d5), which is at the initial stages of the inflammatory SASP (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Day 5 (d5) is at the initial stages of the inflammatory SASP.
source: To determine whether this was the case, we assessed NF-κB nuclear localisation at two earlier timepoints: day 3 (d3), which is before SASP induction and occurs when the cells are coming out of the initial highly proliferative state (Young et al., 2009), and day 5 (d5), which is at the initial stages of the inflammatory SASP (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental design and prior knowledge.

claim: There was no change in NF-κB nucleocytoplasmic ratio at d5 between any of the samples.
source: There was no change in NF-κB nucleocytoplasmic ratio at d5 between any of the samples, and only a small increase between STOP siCTRL and RAS siCTRL at d3 (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, Figure 3—source data 1), suggesting that these timepoints may be too early to observe significant NF-κB nuclear translocation.
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There was only a small increase in NF-κB nucleocytoplasmic ratio between STOP siCTRL and RAS siCTRL at d3.
source: There was no change in NF-κB nucleocytoplasmic ratio at d5 between any of the samples, and only a small increase between STOP siCTRL and RAS siCTRL at d3 (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, Figure 3—source data 1), suggesting that these timepoints may be too early to observe significant NF-κB nuclear translocation.
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: d3 and d5 may be too early to observe significant NF-κB nuclear translocation.
source: There was no change in NF-κB nucleocytoplasmic ratio at d5 between any of the samples, and only a small increase between STOP siCTRL and RAS siCTRL at d3 (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, Figure 3—source data 1), suggesting that these timepoints may be too early to observe significant NF-κB nuclear translocation.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of significant changes in nucleocytoplasmic ratio.

claim: Nuclear NF-κB intensity in the cell was increased in OIS-induced RAS cells compared with the control STOP cells at both d3 and d5.
source: However, nuclear NF-κB intensity in the cell was increased in OIS-induced RAS cells compared with the control STOP cells at both d3 and d5, suggesting early NF-κB activation (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Knockdown of TPR led to significantly lower nuclear NF-κB intensities in RAS cells at both d3 and d5.
source: Knockdown of TPR led to significantly lower nuclear NF-κB intensities in RAS cells at both timepoints, suggesting early NF-κB signalling is reduced when OIS is induced in the absence of TPR.
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Early NF-κB signalling is reduced when OIS is induced in the absence of TPR.
source: Knockdown of TPR led to significantly lower nuclear NF-κB intensities in RAS cells at both timepoints, suggesting early NF-κB signalling is reduced when OIS is induced in the absence of TPR.
evidence: This is inferred from the decreased nuclear NF-κB intensity upon TPR knockdown.

claim: TPR knockdown resulted in decreased NF-κB phosphorylation (S536) in RAS cells at both d3 and d5.
source: Consistent with an effect on early NF-κB activation, immunoblotting showed that TPR knockdown resulted in decreased NF-κB phosphorylation (S536) in RAS cells at both d3 and d5 (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), and decreased phosphorylation of IKK, the upstream kinase (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: TPR knockdown resulted in decreased phosphorylation of IKK in RAS cells at d3 and d5.
source: Consistent with an effect on early NF-κB activation, immunoblotting showed that TPR knockdown resulted in decreased NF-κB phosphorylation (S536) in RAS cells at both d3 and d5 (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), and decreased phosphorylation of IKK, the upstream kinase (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: There was no effect of TPR knockdown on total levels of IKKα at d3 and d5.
source: There was no effect of TPR knockdown on total levels of IKKα at these early timepoints.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: TPR plays a role in NF-κB activation during the early stages of stress in response to oncogenic RAS, before activation of the SASP and without affecting chromatin accessibility at regulatory elements.
source: These data suggest that TPR plays a role in NF-κB activation during the early stages of stress in response to oncogenic RAS, before activation of the SASP and without affecting chromatin accessibility at regulatory elements.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TPR knockdown decreases NF-κB activation at d3 and d5 without affecting chromatin accessibility at these timepoints.

claim: Through its interaction with the TREX-2 complex, TPR is known to be required for the export of intronless and intron-poor mRNAs, as well as histone mRNAs.
source: Through its interaction with the TREX-2 complex, TPR is known to be required for the export of intronless and intron-poor mRNAs, as well as histone mRNAs, the majority of which are intronless (Aksenova et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The majority of histone mRNAs are intronless.
source: Through its interaction with the TREX-2 complex, TPR is known to be required for the export of intronless and intron-poor mRNAs, as well as histone mRNAs, the majority of which are intronless (Aksenova et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: Of the genes downregulated on TPR knockdown, 14% (STOP) or 13% (RAS) are intronless.
source: Indeed, of the genes downregulated on TPR knockdown, 14% (STOP) or 13% (RAS) are intronless (Fisher's exact test, p=1.2 × 10–11; p=7.1 × 10–9, respectively) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Downregulated genes upon TPR knockdown include histone genes (STOP cells: 3 genes, p=6.1 × 10–3; RAS cells: 6 genes, p=4.2 × 10–6).
source: This includes histone genes (STOP cells: 3 genes, p=6.1 × 10–3; RAS cells: 6 genes, p=4.2 × 10–6) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: TPR was the most significantly downregulated gene when comparing siTPR with siCTRL in both RAS and STOP cells.
source: TPR was the most significantly downregulated gene when comparing siTPR with siCTRL in both RAS and STOP cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: STING1 showed the most significant RAS-specific decrease in expression upon TPR knockdown.
source: Interestingly, STING1 showed the most significant RAS-specific decrease in expression (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Reduced STING1 mRNA in RAS cells after 3 days of RAS induction and TPR knockdown was validated by RT-qPCR.
source: Reduced STING1 mRNA in RAS cells after 3 days of RAS induction and TPR knockdown was validated by RT-qPCR (Figure 4B, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Decreased levels of STING protein were consistently detected by d5 of RAS induction upon TPR knockdown.
source: Immunoblotting did not reproducibly detect reduced levels of STING protein at d3 of RAS induction, perhaps due to protein stability at this short timepoint, but decreased levels were consistently detected by d5 (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The cGAS-STING pathway is known to activate the SASP via NF-κB signalling.
source: The cGAS-STING pathway is known to activate the SASP via NF-κB signalling (Dou et al., 2017; Glück et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: cGAS-STING detects dsDNA in the cytoplasm, with DNA binding leading to production of 2′3′ cyclic GMP-AMP (cGAMP), a potent STING agonist.
source: cGAS-STING detects dsDNA in the cytoplasm, with DNA binding leading to production of 2′3′ cyclic GMP-AMP (cGAMP), a potent STING agonist.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the cGAS-STING pathway.

claim: cGAS-independent STING activation has been reported.
source: However, cGAS-independent STING activation has also been reported (Unterholzner and Dunphy, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: cGAMP was significantly elevated in RAS compared with STOP cells.
source: cGAMP was significantly elevated in RAS compared with STOP cells.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: TPR knockdown in RAS cells appeared to result in decreased cGAMP, though this did not reach statistical significance.
source: TPR knockdown in RAS cells appeared to result in decreased cGAMP, though this did not reach statistical significance (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1) acts downstream of STING-mediated sensing of cytosolic DNA, and controls NF-κB signalling.
source: TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1) acts downstream of STING-mediated sensing of cytosolic DNA, and controls NF-κB signalling.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the cGAS-STING-TBK1 pathway.

claim: TBK1 is phosphorylated at serine 172 when active.
source: TBK1 is phosphorylated at serine 172 when active (Abe and Barber, 2014; Shu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: Immunoblotting showed decreased TBK1 phosphorylation in RAS cells upon TPR knockdown at d5 of RAS induction.
source: Immunoblotting showed decreased TBK1 phosphorylation in RAS cells upon TPR knockdown at d5 of RAS induction (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: TPR knockdown blunts STING activation, likely involving cGAS-dependent cytosolic DNA sensing.
source: Together, these data are consistent with TPR knockdown blunting STING activation, likely involving cGAS-dependent cytosolic DNA sensing.
evidence: This is inferred from the decreased STING expression, cGAMP production, and TBK1 phosphorylation upon TPR knockdown.

claim: The transcription of several classes of retrotransposons, including long-interspersed element-1 (LINE1) and human endogenous retroviruses (HERVs), is known to be activated in senescent cells.
source: The transcription of several classes of retrotransposons, including long-interspersed element-1 (LINE1) and human endogenous retroviruses (HERVs), is known to be activated in senescent cells, and sensed through cGAS triggering an innate immune response (De Cecco et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Retrotransposon transcripts in senescent cells are sensed through cGAS triggering an innate immune response.
source: The transcription of several classes of retrotransposons, including long-interspersed element-1 (LINE1) and human endogenous retroviruses (HERVs), is known to be activated in senescent cells, and sensed through cGAS triggering an innate immune response (De Cecco et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: RNA abundance for some transposable elements, including HERV and LINE1 elements, was higher in RAS compared with STOP cells treated with control siRNA.
source: Although RNA abundance for some transposable elements, including HERV and LINE1 elements, was higher in RAS compared with STOP cells treated with control siRNA, there were no significant changes in transposable element RNA abundance upon knockdown of TPR in either cell line (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: There were no significant changes in transposable element RNA abundance upon knockdown of TPR in either STOP or RAS cell lines.
source: Although RNA abundance for some transposable elements, including HERV and LINE1 elements, was higher in RAS compared with STOP cells treated with control siRNA, there were no significant changes in transposable element RNA abundance upon knockdown of TPR in either cell line (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: It is not a change in transposable element expression that drives the decrease in innate immune signalling seen upon TPR knockdown at d3 of OIS.
source: This suggests that it is not a change in transposable element expression that drives the decrease in innate immune signalling seen upon TPR knockdown at d3 of OIS.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of change in transposable element expression upon TPR knockdown.

claim: The frequency of detectable CCFs decreased when TPR was knocked down.
source: To determine whether TPR affects CCF generation, we assessed their frequency – as evidenced by the proportion of cells with DAPI-stained foci in the cytoplasm not obviously connected to the nucleus - at d3 and d5 of RAS induction. The frequency of detectable CCFs decreased when TPR was knocked down.
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The decrease in CCF frequency upon TPR knockdown was only statistically significant at d5.
source: Though apparent by d3, this was only statistically significant at d5 (Figure 5A, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 5A.

claim: CCFs form by blebbing off from the nuclear periphery.
source: CCFs form by blebbing off from the nuclear periphery (Ivanov et al., 2013; Miller et al., 2021) and preferentially contain chromatin fragments enriched in the heterochromatin histone modifications (H3K9me3 and H3K27me3) that are abundant in lamina-associated domains at the nuclear periphery (Guelen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: CCFs preferentially contain chromatin fragments enriched in the heterochromatin histone modifications (H3K9me3 and H3K27me3) that are abundant in lamina-associated domains at the nuclear periphery.
source: CCFs form by blebbing off from the nuclear periphery (Ivanov et al., 2013; Miller et al., 2021) and preferentially contain chromatin fragments enriched in the heterochromatin histone modifications (H3K9me3 and H3K27me3) that are abundant in lamina-associated domains at the nuclear periphery (Guelen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: TPR has been suggested to interact with, and affect the organisation of, lamin B1 at the nuclear periphery.
source: TPR has been suggested to interact with, and affect the organisation of, lamin B1 at the nuclear periphery (Fišerová et al., 2019) and there is loss of lamin B1 from the nuclear periphery in senescence (Dou et al., 2015; Freund et al., 2012; Sadaie et al., 2013; Shimi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: There is loss of lamin B1 from the nuclear periphery in senescence.
source: TPR has been suggested to interact with, and affect the organisation of, lamin B1 at the nuclear periphery (Fišerová et al., 2019) and there is loss of lamin B1 from the nuclear periphery in senescence (Dou et al., 2015; Freund et al., 2012; Sadaie et al., 2013; Shimi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: HMGA1 is a chromatin protein bound throughout the genome.
source: However, here we also show decreased CCF formation in OIS RAS cells following knockdown of HMGA1 – a chromatin protein bound throughout the genome (Olan et al., 2024) and not a component of the nuclear periphery per se.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: HMGA1 is not a component of the nuclear periphery per se.
source: However, here we also show decreased CCF formation in OIS RAS cells following knockdown of HMGA1 – a chromatin protein bound throughout the genome (Olan et al., 2024) and not a component of the nuclear periphery per se.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HMGA1.

claim: Knockdown of HMGA1 in RAS cells led to a significant loss of SAHF compared to control knockdown.
source: Consistent with previous reports, knockdown of HMGA1 in RAS cells led to a significant loss of SAHF compared to control knockdown, and to a greater extent than seen for TPR knockdown (Figure 5F–G).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 5G.

claim: HMGA1 depletion was accompanied by a decrease in CCF frequency at d5 similar to that which occurs on TPR knockdown.
source: HMGA1 depletion was accompanied by a decrease in CCF frequency at d5 similar to that which occurs on TPR knockdown (Figure 5H, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The decrease in CCF is linked to changes in heterochromatin organisation, i.e., SAHF formation and not to changes at the nuclear pore basket per se.
source: These data suggest that the decrease in CCF is linked to changes in heterochromatin organisation, i.e., SAHF formation and not to changes at the nuclear pore basket per se.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both TPR and HMGA1, which are required for SAHF formation, are also required for CCF formation.

claim: Heterochromatin is stiffer and more resistant to deformation than euchromatin.
source: Heterochromatin is stiffer and more resistant to deformation than euchromatin (Ghosh et al., 2021) and decreasing heterochromatin by inhibiting histone deacetylases has been shown to increase nuclear blebbing (Stephens et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Decreasing heterochromatin by inhibiting histone deacetylases has been shown to increase nuclear blebbing.
source: Heterochromatin is stiffer and more resistant to deformation than euchromatin (Ghosh et al., 2021) and decreasing heterochromatin by inhibiting histone deacetylases has been shown to increase nuclear blebbing (Stephens et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The decrease in CCFs produced during the early phases of OIS upon TPR, or HMGA1, knockdown is caused by an increase in the stability of the nuclear periphery due to the heterochromatin that remains there when SAHF are not formed.
source: We therefore consider it likely that the decrease in CCFs produced during the early phases of OIS upon TPR, or HMGA1, knockdown is caused by an increase in the stability of the nuclear periphery due to the heterochromatin that remains there when SAHF are not formed.
evidence: This is inferred from the data linking SAHF formation to CCF formation and the known properties of heterochromatin.

claim: TPR has a role in the loss of nuclear integrity that occurs in response to oncogene-induced stress, leading directly to activation of cytoplasmic nucleic acid sensing and the key inflammatory gene expression programme of senescence.
source: Together, our results suggest a role for TPR as an important factor in the loss of nuclear integrity that occurs in response to oncogene-induced stress, leading directly to activation of cytoplasmic nucleic acid sensing and the key inflammatory gene expression programme of senescence.
evidence: This is inferred from the data linking TPR to CCF formation, innate immune signaling, and NF-κB activation.

claim: Cytoplasmic chromatin derived from the nuclear genome is known to activate the innate immune response, sensed and signalled through cGAS-STING upstream of TBK1.
source: Cytoplasmic chromatin derived from the nuclear genome is known to activate the innate immune response, sensed and signalled through cGAS-STING upstream of TBK1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cytoplasmic DNA sensing.

claim: Cytoplasmic DNA sensing is best studied in the context of micronuclei, formed during mitosis as a consequence of unrepaired DNA damage.
source: Cytoplasmic DNA sensing is best studied in the context of micronuclei, formed during mitosis as a consequence of unrepaired DNA damage (Miller et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Micronuclei can contain many different types of chromatin.
source: Micronuclei can contain many different types of chromatin (Mammel et al., 2022) and have been reported to have NPCs in their membrane, albeit at a much lower density than the primary nuclear membrane (Crasta et al., 2012; Hatch et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Micronuclei have been reported to have NPCs in their membrane, albeit at a much lower density than the primary nuclear membrane.
source: Micronuclei can contain many different types of chromatin (Mammel et al., 2022) and have been reported to have NPCs in their membrane, albeit at a much lower density than the primary nuclear membrane (Crasta et al., 2012; Hatch et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: We could not detect a core nuclear pore component (POM121), or TPR, in CCFs.
source: In contrast, we could not detect a core nuclear pore component (POM121), or TPR, in CCFs, consistent with a mechanism of formation that is distinct from that of micronuclei.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C-E.

claim: The mechanism of CCF formation is distinct from that of micronuclei.
source: In contrast, we could not detect a core nuclear pore component (POM121), or TPR, in CCFs, consistent with a mechanism of formation that is distinct from that of micronuclei.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of nuclear pore components in CCFs.

claim: Either the CCFs are formed from the nuclear membrane between NPCs or NPCs are rapidly lost from CCFs.
source: This suggests that either the CCFs are formed from the nuclear membrane between NPCs or that NPCs are rapidly lost from CCFs.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of nuclear pore components in CCFs.

claim: CCFs contain lamin B1.
source: CCFs are known to contain lamin B1 (Dou et al., 2015) but whether they contain other components of the nuclear envelope is unexplored.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: CCFs appear to lack staining for TPR or for POM121, suggesting that there are no nuclear pores in the CCF envelope.
source: However, they appear to lack staining for TPR or for POM121, a transmembrane nucleoporin, suggesting that there are no nuclear pores in the CCF envelope (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C-E.

claim: Lowered NF-κB activity upon TPR knockdown during early RAS activation (d3) is not accompanied by changes in chromatin accessibility at the putative enhancers of SASP genes.
source: To determine whether, as at d8, lowered NF-κB activity upon TPR knockdown during early RAS activation (d3) is accompanied by changes in chromatin accessibility at the putative enhancers of SASP genes, we carried out ATAC-seq on STOP and RAS cells treated with 4-OHT for 3 days, as well as with control and TPR siRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: Some of the accessible regions defined as senescence specific (SEN+) at d8 also show senescence-specific enhanced chromatin accessibility at d3, albeit less marked than at d8.
source: Whilst some of the accessible regions defined as senescence specific (SEN+) at d8 also show senescence-specific enhanced chromatin accessibility at d3, albeit less marked than at d8, SEN+ accessibility peaks that were TPR-dependent (TPR+) at d8 did not show decreased chromatin accessibility upon TPR knockdown at d3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: SEN+ accessibility peaks that were TPR-dependent (TPR+) at d8 did not show decreased chromatin accessibility upon TPR knockdown at d3.
source: Whilst some of the accessible regions defined as senescence specific (SEN+) at d8 also show senescence-specific enhanced chromatin accessibility at d3, albeit less marked than at d8, SEN+ accessibility peaks that were TPR-dependent (TPR+) at d8 did not show decreased chromatin accessibility upon TPR knockdown at d3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: No TPR-dependent (TPR+) senescence-specific (SEN+) ATAC-seq peaks were identified at d3.
source: Indeed, we identified no TPR-dependent (TPR+) senescence-specific (SEN+) ATAC-seq peaks at d3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: The d3 RAS-specific peaks were enriched for AP-1 binding motifs, similar to the d8 TPR+SEN+ peaks.
source: Motif analysis showed that the d3 RAS-specific peaks were enriched for AP-1 binding motifs, similar to the d8 TPR+SEN+ peaks (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: d3 RAS-specific peaks are in proximity to genes involved in SAHF regulation, as well as TGF-β signalling.
source: GO analysis showed that d3 RAS-specific peaks are in proximity to genes involved in SAHF regulation, as well as TGF-β signalling, which has been implicated in the early NOTCH1 regulated SASP (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E; Hoare et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E.

claim: TGF-β signalling has been implicated in the early NOTCH1 regulated SASP.
source: GO analysis showed that d3 RAS-specific peaks are in proximity to genes involved in SAHF regulation, as well as TGF-β signalling, which has been implicated in the early NOTCH1 regulated SASP (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E; Hoare et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: TPR loss during OIS (d8) prevents chromatin opening at putative SASP gene enhancers enriched in binding motifs for NF-κB.
source: We show that TPR loss during OIS (d8) prevents chromatin opening at putative SASP gene enhancers enriched in binding motifs for NF-κB – a key TF that drives the SASP.
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data showing decreased accessibility at NF-κB motif-enriched peaks upon TPR knockdown at d8.

claim: TPR loss has its impact upstream of NF-κB and its translocation to the nucleus, by decreasing TBK1 phosphorylation, likely downstream of cGAS-STING signalling.
source: Rather, our data suggest that TPR loss has its impact upstream of NF-κB and its translocation to the nucleus, by decreasing TBK1 phosphorylation, likely downstream of cGAS-STING signalling.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing decreased TBK1 phosphorylation, STING expression, and cGAMP production upon TPR knockdown.
